It's a Sunday in April. Little Ludwig has been christened, and Mara is his godmother. Everyone is celebrating in the courtyard on Kastanienallee, under the chestnut tree that is in bloom. Andrei has one more week in Berlin; then he's going back to Sibiu until the autumn.
Ludwig, have you got a moment? I want to tell you something before I leave.
I always have a moment for you, my boy. Sit down. The bench is still warm from the sun.
I wanted to thank you. For everything. For the stories, for the city, for the brown notebook. Without you I would never have really got to know Berlin.
Nonsense. You got to know it on your own. I just showed you where to listen. So? Did you get the acceptance from the university?
Yes! This morning. From October I'm doing my master's here. Two years.
That's the best news in a long time. Does Lena know yet?
Not yet. I wanted to tell you first. And I wanted to ask you… the longer I stay here, the more I feel at home. Is that normal?
Of course. Home isn't a place, my boy. Home is people. The more people you love, the more “homes” you have.
I'm writing that in the notebook. On the last page.
No. Not on the last page. The notebook is still far from full. You're coming back in October and then we'll keep writing. Promise?
I promise. And now I'm going to Lena. Wish me luck.
You don't need luck, my boy. You only have to ask. She'll do the rest. Your sister said that once, and most of the time she's right.

“danken” takes the dative for the person and “für + accusative” for the thing: “Ich danke dir (Dat.) für den Kuchen (Akk.).”
Replies to thanks: “Bitte!”, “Gern geschehen!” (you're welcome), “Nichts zu danken!” (don't mention it), “Keine Ursache!”.

“je + comparative” introduces a subordinate clause (verb at the END), and “desto + comparative” starts the main clause (verb straight after it):
The more you practise, the better you speak.
The older he gets, the calmer he is.
The short form, without verbs: “Je früher, desto besser.” = The sooner, the better. “Je mehr, desto lustiger.” = The more, the merrier.

Little Ludwig's christening took place on a warm Sunday in April, in the old Gethsemane Church in Prenzlauer Berg, just five minutes from Kastanienallee. Ludwig told everyone who wanted to hear that in this church, in the autumn of 1989, people had prayed with candles for freedom, and that back then he had passed by every evening on the tram and seen the candles multiply day after day.

Mara stood next to the font, in a light green dress, with little Ludwig in her arms. He was four months old now, had thick red hair and laughed at everything: at the light from the coloured stained-glass windows, at the priest with the long beard, at Fritz, who was sitting in the last row, even though dogs weren't actually allowed in the church. The priest had just smiled and said: “A dog who sits so quietly is welcome here.”

When the priest poured the water over the baby's head, little Ludwig didn't scream. He looked at Mara, serious and surprised, and then he grabbed her finger and held it tight. Mara thought of the night in January, more than two years ago, when she had bandaged Jonas's burnt hand. Of the ring in the glove. Of everything that had happened since then. The more she thought about it, the more incredible it seemed to her.

After church, everyone celebrated in the courtyard. The chestnut tree was in bloom for the first time that year, with hundreds of white candle-shaped blossoms, and under it stood the long table with the white tablecloth, as on every big day in this house. Lena had baked a cake in the shape of a church, Kasia had made pierogi, Mara's mother had sent a parcel of cozonac (Romanian sweet bread) from Sibiu, and Thomas had come with his whole family from Munich. Paul had his guitar with him. He now played almost as well as his grandfather. At least that's what his grandfather said.

Mrs Hoffmann sat at her window on the fourth floor, in the grey blanket. Since the pneumonia in February she no longer came down the stairs, not even on a chair. But she had opened the window wide and pushed the piano as close as possible, with Piotr's help. And when little Ludwig was carried into the courtyard, she began to play. Not Chopin this time, but a lullaby. The same Brahms lullaby she had played on the night he was born.

Towards evening, Mara saw Andrei get up and go over to Lena, who was just cutting the cake. He said something to her quietly. Lena put the knife down. She looked at him. Then she screamed so loudly that Fritz and Bruno barked at the same time, and little Ludwig started laughing from the fright. She threw her arms around Andrei's neck, with cream on her hands, and everyone in the courtyard knew at once what had happened. Andrei was coming back in October. For two years. Maybe for longer.

Kuba climbed onto a chair and shouted: “The more people live in this house, the better!” Everyone laughed and clapped. Ola added: “And the more dogs, the better!” Bruno barked in approval. Ludwig raised his glass.

A little earlier, Mara's phone had rung. It was a video call from Sibiu. Her parents were sitting in the garden, under the old apple tree, which was also just coming into bloom, and waving at the camera. Her father was holding up a little jar: the lime-blossom honey from the roof of Kastanienallee 35, which Ludwig and Klaus had given him in May. He hadn't eaten it. Since then it had stood on the shelf in the living room, next to the photo of Mara as a child. Mara turned the phone round so that her parents could see the courtyard: the chestnut tree in bloom, the long table, the crowd of people, Lena with cream on her hands, Andrei, who went red when his mother shouted “Congratulations!”. Her mother cried, of course. Her father said a single sentence, in Romanian, and Mara translated it for everyone: “He says the bees have found a new home. And that it's good this way.”

Dear friends. Dear neighbours. Dear family. I'm eighty years old and I've seen a lot in my life. A wall that was built and a wall that fell. A city in ruins and a city that dances again. I loved a woman and I lost her. And I thought that after her nothing beautiful would come.
He paused. The courtyard was completely silent. Only up on the fourth floor did the piano go on playing softly.

Then, one evening, a young woman from Sibiu rang my doorbell. She only wanted the keys. She gave me much more. She explained a phone to me, showed me a concert hall, gave me back a tram and a son I talk to again. Thank you, Mara. For everything. The older I get, the better I understand what Ingrid always used to say: life is a circle. What you give comes back. Sometimes from Sibiu.

Mara couldn't say anything. She was holding little Ludwig in her arms and crying, and little Ludwig was reaching for her tears, as if it were a game. Lena hugged her from the left, Andrei from the right, and then all the others came: Jonas and Clara, Kuba and Ola, Kasia and Piotr, Thomas and Paul, Klaus and Mr Wolff, who had come in uniform, and Dr Yılmaz with her guitar. A circle of people under a chestnut tree in bloom.

Up on the fourth floor, the piano stopped. Mrs Hoffmann leaned out of the window as far as she could and called down into the courtyard in her thin, clear voice: “And if they haven't died!” And the whole courtyard, fifty people, two dogs and a baby, shouted back: “They're still alive today!”

In the evening, after everyone had left, Andrei opened the brown notebook at the next empty page. He wrote the date. Then he wrote, slowly, in German, without a single mistake: “Home isn't a place. Home is people. To be continued in October.”
Then he switched off the light. Downstairs, on the first floor, the yellow lamp was still burning, as it did every evening. And up on the fourth floor, a window stood open.

Reading text: Mara's letter to Ludwig
Read the note Mara left under Ludwig's door after the christening. Listen twice. At the end there are 4 questions.
Dear Ludwig, today you thanked me in front of everyone. Now it's my turn to thank you, just on paper, because I'd cry if I had to say it to you.
When I came to Berlin, I had two suitcases, three jars of honey and an awful lot of fear.
You gave me the keys. But you also gave me the city, your stories and your language. The better I speak German, the better I understand how much you've taught me.
I wish you many more years under the yellow lamp, lots of games of chess with Klaus (you'll win one day!) and lots of Sundays with little Ludwig.
Thank you for everything. Your Mara from the third floor. PS: Fritz got three frankfurters today. It wasn't me.
